planting.note: Soak seed 24 hours before direct-sowing in spring into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; avoid rich or heavily amended beds, which cause floppy growth.

directions: An early colonizer of disturbed sandy ground across the Gulf South, this fine-textured bunchgrass is valued for rapid erosion control and for the reddish-maroon cast its panicles take on in late summer, giving the plant its common name. It thrives in lean, sandy, well-drained soil and declines in rich or moist beds. Leave seed heads standing through winter for birds rather than cutting back in fall.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide - Red Lovegrass

planting.note: Direct-sow in spring into seasonally moist, sandy, acidic soil; tolerates part shade better than most lovegrasses, so a naturalistic pine-savanna understory planting suits it well.

directions: A fire-adapted tufted grass of pine savannas, flatwoods, and moist pinelands from Delaware to Texas, this species mimics open-understory conditions when used in naturalistic southeastern pine-savanna plantings. Many wild populations rely on periodic burning for vigor, so an occasional hard cutback in late winter serves the same renewing purpose in a garden setting. It performs best in seasonally moist, sandy, acidic soil rather than rich garden loam.

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant in spring into nutrient-poor sandy or limestone soil in full sun; needs no supplemental fertilizer and performs worse in rich garden soil.

directions: A fast-growing clumping bluestem of Florida and southeastern Coastal Plain pine rocklands and sandhills, thriving in nutrient-poor sandy or limestone soil without supplemental fertilizer. Nearly as broad as it is tall in foliage, it sends up conspicuous silvery-white bearded flower stalks in late summer and fall. Best suited to naturalistic restorations and dry, low-fertility sites; rich garden soil causes weak, floppy growth.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation - Natives for Your Neighborhood

planting.note: Fall-sow for natural cold stratification (needs roughly 60 days) into moist, sandy soil in part sun; the rhizomatous habit suits bank stabilization and shaded wet-meadow plantings.

directions: Found naturally in moist-to-wet sandy pinelands, maritime forests, and ditches across the southeastern US, this grass gets its common name from the distinctive arching second glume that gives each spikelet a beaked look. Its rhizomatous habit makes it useful for bank stabilization and shaded wet-meadow plantings where many ornamental grasses struggle, and the seed is a good food source for upland birds and waterfowl. It flowers best with several hours of direct sun even though it tolerates part shade better than most warm-season panicgrasses.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet - Beaked Panicgrass

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant in spring into consistently moist clay or wet soil in full to part sun; does not tolerate extended drought, especially in the first growing season.

directions: A robust wetland bunchgrass of marshes, ditches, floodplain woods, and pond margins across the eastern US, with reddish-purple inflorescences from midsummer through fall. It tolerates standing water and poorly drained clay as well as average garden soil, making it a reliable choice for rain gardens and pond edges where most ornamental grasses rot out. Keep soil consistently moist, since it does not tolerate extended drought.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation - Natives for Your Neighborhood
